Psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; and he makes an antithesis between the hilarity arising from drunkenness and the holy hilarity which arises in the assembly of the pious from pious songs and Psalms. Moreover, when he says "in the heart," the Apostle does not intend that each should sing internally and to himself without the tongue, but he requires a serious affection of the heart.

Therefore, two things ought to be joined in the songs of the pious: a pious affection of the heart, and a tongue that serves to excite the affections. Let these things be said regarding the manner of hilarity.

The time of staying at a feast should not be dragged out to the beginning of madness, but only to the middle of hilarity, especially for a pastor, upon whom others cast their eyes.

Nothing is more foul, or can be said to be so, than for a pastor to drain cups of madness and be the last one to leave home. To me, he who is such a one seems unworthy to have care of goats, let alone the sheep of Christ. By the apostle Jude, such as these are called spots in brotherly feasts, as those who, for pleasure, live in luxury for a day, miserably staining themselves and offering an occasion for spots to others.

Now the situation demands that we prescribe the discipline which the pastor must keep in contracts.

Therefore, first let the pastor beware that he does not seek sordid gain, or, as Paul says, that he not be <term>aischokerdes</term> <gloss>shamefully greedy for gain</gloss>.

### OF M. FRIDERICUS SCHINDLER,
#### Co-Rector of the School of Schneeberg.

<note>A decorative initial capital letter H with foliate ornamentation.</note>

Here where Bohemia touches the Sudetes mountains,
And separates the Mysians <note>likely referring to local inhabitants or a poetic reference to the region</note> from its borders thence.
Here the fields are most ample with silver-bearing veins,
The land abounds with superb-making bronze.
Here where you see the ant <note>the miners</note> carry the pure metals
Scattered through the viscera of the earth in a hollow log.
The windings of the earth, thus the splendid temples are seen,
Where the city named from the snowy mountain lies.
Rightly does the Mount of Anne and the Mount of Mary yield to you,
Freiberg itself and the Valley give you glory.
*c* The abundant supply of your vein overcame all things,
When your Mountain was in honor at the first.
The sword-bearing Elector, that Johannes Georgius the Second,
The pillar and safeguard of the Saxon House,
Considers calling his spirit back from troublesome cares,
And of his own accord to enter the houses of the Snowy Mountain,
Leaving Dresden <note>d</note> accompanied by a troop of horsemen
*e* He comes here, and with the pomp which is usual for Dukes.
The knights precede in order with radiant arms,
The clear trumpets give forth sound with a warning voice.

---

27. PAULUS, book 28 of the Edict.
He who pays what is not owed, thinking he owes it in a certain place, shall recover it in any place: for the same mode of recovery does not follow the belief of the one paying.

If a debtor has paid after being acquitted.
28. THE SAME, book 32 of the Edict.
If a judge has acquitted someone wrongly, and the person acquitted pays of his own accord, he cannot recover it.

Regarding a ward, a madman, and a prodigal.
29. ULPIANUS, book 2 of the Disputations.
Sometimes the person creates room for recovery: for example, if a ward without the authority of his tutor, or a madman, or one to whom his property has been interdicted, has paid: for it is not doubted that in these persons there is generally room for recovery: and if the coins still exist, they will be vindicated: but if they have been consumed, a claim for recovery will have a place.

Regarding one who is both a creditor and a debtor.
30. THE SAME, book 10 of the Disputations.
He who is in turn a creditor and also a debtor, in cases where compensation does not apply, if he pays, does not have a claim for recovery as for an undue payment, but a petition for his own credit.

Regarding an undue promise.
31. THE SAME, book 1 of the Opinions.
He who, by mistake, has provided a guarantee to a creditor for more than the hereditary portion amounts to, has a claim for recovery of an undue promise.

<column-break/>

Regarding an alternate obligation. 1. Regarding a surety. 2. Regarding what a woman gave in the name of a dowry. 3. Regarding an obligation of kind.
32. JULIANUS, book 10 of the Digest.
When he who owes Pamphilus or Stichus has paid both at once, if after he has paid both, either both or one of them ceases to exist in the nature of things, he shall recover nothing: for that which remains will stay in the payment.
§ 1. When a surety makes a pact that money not be sought from him, and through imprudence he pays, he will be able to make a claim for recovery against the stipulator; and therefore the principal debtor remains obligated, but he himself is safe by his own exception: nor does it matter whether the surety or his heir pays: but if the principal debtor should be heir to this surety and pays, he will neither recover it, nor will he be released.
§ 2. If a woman is of the opinion that she is obligated for a dowry, whatever she gives in the name of a dowry she shall not recover: for once the false opinion is removed, there remains the cause of duty, from which a payment made cannot be recovered.
§ 3. He who has promised a man in general is similar to him who owes a man or ten: and therefore, if, when he thought he had promised Stichus, he gave him, he shall have a claim for recovery: but by giving any other one, he will be able to release himself.

Puta esse quod dicis: & effundi verba non fingi. Primum habet ista res suam gratiam: & est decor proprius orationis leniter lapsæ. Multum enim interest existimo vtrum exciderit, an fluxerit. Nunc in hoc quoque quod dicturus sum, ingens differentia est. Fabianus mihi non effundere videtur orationem, sed fundere, adeo larga est, & sine perturbatione, non fine cursu tamen, veniens. illud planè fatetur & præfert, non esse se tractatam, nec diu tortam, sed ita vt eius esse credamus. Præterea ipso dicēte non vacasset tibi partes intueri: adeo te summa rapuisset, & ferè quæ impetu placent, minus præstát ad manum relata. Some remedies beneficial to other parts of the body cannot be applied to others, as they are foul and indecorous, and what would benefit elsewhere without loss of modesty becomes dishonest at the site of a wound. Does it not shame you to heal mourning with pleasure? Such things must be healed more severely. Rather, advise yourself of this: that no sense of evil reaches him who perishes. For if it reaches him, he has not perished. Nothing, I say, harms him who is nothing. He lives, if he is harmed. Do you think it is bad for him because he is nothing, or because he is still something? But yet, there cannot be torment for him from the fact that he is not; for who is of no sense? Nor from the fact that he is. For he escapes the greatest disadvantage of death, which is not to be. Let us also say to him who laments and longs for one snatched away in the first age: We are all, as far as the brevity of time is concerned, if you compare it to the universe, both young and old, on an equal footing. For less comes to us from all of time than what one would call the least; since, indeed, the least is some part. This that we live is closest to nothing; and yet, because of our madness, it is arranged widely. I have written these things to you, not as if you were expecting a remedy from me so fierce—for it is clear to me that you have spoken with yourself whatever you are about to read—but so that I might chastise that slight delay by which you retreated from yourself and, for the remainder, might exhort you that you would lift your spirits against fortune and foresee all its weapons, not as if they could come, but as if they were certainly going to come.

EP. 100. You write that you have read the books of Fabianus Papirius, which are titled "Cinilium," most eagerly, but that they did not answer to your expectation. Then, forgetting that they are a composition of philosophy, you accuse their structure. Suppose it is as you say: and that words are poured out, not fashioned. First, that matter has its own grace; and there is a propriety proper to speech that has slipped along gently. For I think it makes a great difference whether it has fallen out or has flowed. Now, in this too, which I am about to say, there is a huge difference. Fabianus does not seem to me to pour out speech, but to dispense it; so large is it, and coming without perturbation, though not without speed. That, he plainly confesses and puts forward, that it was not labored over, nor long twisted, but so that we might believe it to be of him. He composed his character, not his words; and he wrote those things for the mind, not for the ears. Besides, when he was speaking, you would not have had the leisure to observe the parts; so much would the sum have carried you away, and things that please by their impetus are almost less effective when brought back to hand. But that too is much, to have occupied the eyes at the first aspect, even if diligent contemplation is going to find something to argue against. If you ask me, he is greater who has carried off the judgment than he who has merited it. And I know that the latter is safer; I know that he promises more boldly to himself about the future. Anxious speech does not befit a philosopher. Where, in the end, will he be strong and constant, where will he put himself to the test, who fears words? Fabianus was not negligent in speech, but secure. Therefore, you will find nothing sordid. Strange indeed. What did that woman know, yet she was as magnificent and extraordinary as this? How beautiful the character of Qiao Niang is; her virtue is truly complete. She did not serve two husbands, which is chastity. She sought to repay the one who understood her, which is righteousness. She stepped forward to confront the officials, which is courage. She cried and pleaded with shrinking humility, which is wisdom. She endured poverty without being tainted, which is integrity. She raised the child from infancy and taught him as he grew, which is benevolence and propriety. Even after her death, she was still able to stop her coffin and rebuke her son, eventually succeeding in her wish to be buried in her original home. She was a perfected person in the underworld. Alas, how miraculous!
